en: Therīgāthā 16.1 Mahānipāta:
The Stanzas of the Elder Nun Sumedhā
In the city of Mantāvati,
I was the daughter of Koñca, the chief queen of the king. I was Sumedhā.
She was inspired by those who carry out the Teaching—
virtuous, eloquent in speech,
learned in the Buddha’s Dispensation, and well-disciplined.
Approaching his mother and father, he said: "Listen, both of you;
I am one who delights in Nibbāna."
Even if the state of existence were eternal, even if it were celestial—
how much more so then these empty sensual pleasures,
which offer little gratification and bring much affliction?
Sensual pleasures are bitter,
like poison, yet in them fools are infatuated;
they shall dwell in hell for a long time.
Overwhelmed and afflicted, they are slain;
those of evil deeds grieve,
ever increasing their wickedness in the states of woe.
The fools are unrestrained in body, speech, and mind;
those fools are of poor wisdom.
Lacking consciousness, they are stirred up by suffering and its origin;
not understanding when it is being taught,
they do not awaken to the Noble Truths.
O mother, those who do not understand the Truths taught by the excellent Buddha are more numerous than those who rejoice in existence.
They long for rebirth among the devas.
Yet even rebirth among the devas is impermanent within the cycle of existence, which is itself unstable.
But fools do not find peace,
for they must be born again and again.
There are four states of ruin.
Two destinies can somehow be attained;
but for those who have gone to the states of ruin,
there is no going forth in the hells.
"Grant me permission, both of you,
to go forth in the teaching of the One of Ten Powers;
free from anxiety, I shall strive."
For the sake of abandoning birth and death,
what is the use of delighting in existence,
which is a worthless and insubstantial bodily ruin?
With the cessation of craving for existence, grant me permission; I shall go forth.
The appearance of Buddhas has been missed.
The opportune moment has been found;
may I not violate my moral precepts and the holy life for as long as I live.
Thus spoke Sumedhā to her parents:
"I shall not take food as long as I am a householder."
"I shall surely fall under the power of death.
Thus the mother weeps in suffering and the father as well,
for her life has been utterly struck down.
They strove to awaken him, who had fallen from the palace floor to the ground:
"Arise, my son! Why do you grieve?"
You were given by him in Vāraṇavatī;
you were given to King Anīkaratta, who is handsome.
"You shall become the chief queen,
the consort of King Anikaratta;
[you shall observe] the moral precepts and the holy life."
"Going forth is difficult, my son.
In kingship there is command, wealth, and sovereignty;
enjoyments are pleasant, and you are still young."
"Enjoy the pleasures of the senses;
let there be a wedding for you, my son.
Then Sumedhā spoke to them:
“Let there be no such worthless states of existence;
whether it be renunciation or death, I shall certainly not turn back.”
Why indeed would one enter this putrid body— impure, smelling of raw flesh, terrifying,
a mere corpse, and like a bellows?
Constantly oozing and filled with impurity—
how can you, knowing it thus,
[be attached to] this loathsome thing, smeared with flesh and blood?
This body, a dwelling for worms and food for birds— of what use is it?
It is carried away to the charnel ground.
Before long, the body, devoid of consciousness,
will be cast aside like a log by relatives who feel revulsion.
Having cast him into the charnel ground,
his own parents, feeling loathing, bathe after the meal.
But what of the common folk?
They are attached to this worthless physical body, a mere collection of bones and sinews.
In this putrid body,
filled with spittle and excrement,
he who can dissect it—
One should make the outside like the inside;
even one’s own mother would feel disgust for a person who cannot endure the smell.
The aggregates, elements,
and sense-bases are conditioned, rooted in birth, and suffering;
reflecting upon them with systematic wisdom, one [sees this].
Whom would one desire as a bridegroom?
Even if nine hundred and ninety-three arrows were to fall upon my body day after day;
Even a hundred years of killing are better than this:
the destruction of suffering.
One should accept such killing.
Whoever understands this word of the Teacher:
"Long is their saṃsāra,
as they are slain again and again."
Among gods and humans,
in the animal realm and the host of asuras;
among the hungry ghosts and in the hells.
Immeasurable killings are seen;
many killings occur for one who has gone to the states of ruin and is being tormented in the hells.
Even among the gods,
there is no self other than Nibbāna-happiness.
They have attained that Nibbāna.
Those who are devoted to the word of the One of Ten Powers,
being free from anxiety,
strive for the abandoning of birth and death.
"Father, let me go forth this very day!
What is the use of these worthless enjoyments?
I am weary of sensual pleasures."
"Reduced to a state like vomit, made as worthless as a palm leaf.
While she was speaking thus to her father,
the one to whom she had been given was the one who possessed the luster of a jewel.
He went to Vāraṇavata when the time for the wedding had arrived; then, [he saw] the food that was not yet eaten,
the water that was not yet drunk, and the garments that were not yet worn.
Having cut through his hair with a sword,
Sumedha closed the palace gate and attained the first jhāna.
And she was absorbed in that meditative attainment there,
while Anīkaratta arrived at the city;
and Sumedhā was in the palace.
He develops the perception of impermanence. He attends to it,
and the night-watcher ascended quickly.
With his body adorned with jewels and gold,
he joined his palms in reverence and entreated Sumedha:
“In my kingdom, [I offer] the wealth of my commands— ”
Your infatuation with pleasures was but slight when you were young;
enjoy the objects of sensual desire,
for sensual happiness is difficult to find in the world.
Your kingdom has been relinquished;
enjoy your wealth and give gifts;
do not be despondent.
“Your mother and father are suffering,” Sumedhā said to him,
free from delusion and having no desire for sensual pleasures.
"Do not delight in sensual pleasures;
see the peril in sensual pleasures.
Even a king who rules over the four continents..."
Mandhātā was the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures;
he died unsatisfied,
for his desire had not been fulfilled.
Even if the seven treasures were to rain down,
with showers falling from all ten directions on every side,
there would still be no satiety for sensual desires.
Men die still unsatisfied.
Sensual pleasures are like a sword and a butcher’s block;
sensual pleasures are like the hood of a serpent.
Like flames they burn,
resembling a skeleton;
sensual pleasures are impermanent and unstable.
They bring much suffering and are like great poisons;
they are the root of evil with suffering as their fruit, like a red-hot iron ball.
Sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree;
painful, they are like a piece of meat;
deceptive, they are like a dream.
Sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods;
sensual pleasures are like swords and spears;
they are a disease, a boil, a calamity, and a misfortune.
Like pits of glowing coals,
the root of evil, fear, and slaughter—
thus are sensual pleasures full of much suffering.
I have declared these to be obstacles;
go, for I have no confidence in you,
even regarding my own life.
What can another do for me when my own head is burning,
while old age and death pursue me?
"One must strive for his destruction.
Without opening the door,
I [spoke to] my mother, father, and Anīkaratta.
Seeing them sitting on the ground and weeping, I said this:
"Long is the saṃsāra for fools."
And weeping again and again at the deaths of fathers,
brothers, and ourselves throughout the beginningless cycle of existence.
One could not easily measure the tears,
the breast-milk, and the blood shed by beings wandering through this beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
Remember the accumulation of bones;
remember the four oceans when they have been reduced to tears, breast-milk, and blood.
The heap of bones of those who have lived for a single eon would be equal to a vast accumulation;
thus it is for one wandering through the cycle of existence from a beginningless past.
Even if the entire earth of Jambudīpa were brought forward as pellets the size of jujube seeds,
the mothers themselves would not suffice to count them all.
Remember that the grass, sticks, branches,
and foliage brought here from the beginningless cycle of rebirth are like water-pots four finger-breadths high.
Even fathers and grandfathers do not suffice [to repay one's debt].
Remember the blind turtle in the eastern ocean and the yoke-hole in the western ocean.
And his head was covered; this is the simile for obtaining human birth.
Remember that form is like a lump of foam.
This body is a mass of impurities, devoid of essence;
behold the aggregates as impermanent,
and remember the hells with their many afflictions.
Remembering how, in various successive births, one repeatedly increases the forest of thorns,
and remembers the fears of crocodiles.
Contemplate the Four Truths.
While the Deathless exists,
what use have you for drinking the five-fold bitter draught?
For all delights of sensual pleasure are more bitter than the five-fold poison,
even while the Deathless exists.
What use have you for sensual pleasures, which are but fevers?
For all delights of the senses are ablaze,
seething, trembling, and burning.
Since there is equal enmity [in both cases],
what use have you for sensual pleasures which bring many enemies—
[enemies] such as kings, fire, thieves, water, and those who are dear?
Sensual pleasures are common property and bring many enemies.
Since liberation exists,
what use have you for sensual pleasures, in which there is only killing and bondage?
For those who have no desire for sensual pleasures do not experience the sufferings of killing and bondage;
they are like grass-torches that have been set ablaze.
They burn the one who grasps, not the one who lets go;
for sensual pleasures are like a firebrand—
they burn those who do not let them go.
Do not, for the sake of a trifle—
the pleasure of sensual desire— abandon abundant happiness;
do not be like a fish that swallows the hook.
Having swallowed it, you will suffer afterwards.
Subdue your desire for sensual pleasures,
even as a dog bound by a chain.
Sensual pleasures will surely torment you,
like hungry outcasts tormenting a dog;
and there will be immeasurable suffering.
And you will experience many mental sorrows,
being bound to sensual desires; therefore, relinquish these transient pleasures.
While agelessness exists,
what use have you for sensual pleasures, in which there is aging,
and which are seized by death and disease?
All births everywhere have ceased.
This is ageless, this is deathless;
this is the sorrowless state, free from aging and death.
Free from enmity, unconfined,
unshakable, fearless, and without affliction—
this has been attained by many.
This deathless state is still attainable today by one who applies themselves with systematic method;
it is not possible for one who does not exert effort.
Thus spoke Sumedhā,
finding no delight in conditioned things,
entreating him not to depart.
And how did Sumedha cast down the dust?
Rising up, untiring and with palms joined, he made a request to his father.
“Release Sumedhā, O parents,
so that she may go forth and see the truth of liberation.
Having been released by her mother and father,
Fearing sorrow and fear, she went forth;
having realized the six direct knowledges,
the training nun attained the highest fruit.
It was a marvel, a wonder,
that Nibbāna occurred for the royal maiden;
[she remembered] her past lives and conduct.
Just as he prophesied in his final time:
"During the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana,
in a newly established monastery within the Saṅghārāma;..."
We three female friends, O companions,
gave a gift of a monastery;
ten times, a hundred times—
A hundred times a hundred and a thousand times a thousand,
we were reborn among the devas;
what need is there to speak of being born among humans?
Among the gods we possessed great supernormal power;
what need is there to speak of the human realm?
We were the chief queen of one who possessed the seven treasures.
I was the Jewel of Womanhood.
That is the cause, that the source,
that the root, and that indeed is patience within the Teaching.
That is the first convergence;
that is the Nibbāna for one who delights in the Dhamma.
Thus do those who [possess] faith—
They strike down the word of the one of peerless wisdom;
they become disenchanted with the course of existence, and having become disenchanted, they become dispassionate.
Thus indeed did the Elder Nun Sumedhā speak these verses.
The Mahānipāta is finished.
The Therīgāthā is complete.
Four hundred and eighty-four verses;
one hundred and eleven therīs.
"All those [have attained] the destruction of the taints.
The Pāli Text of the Therīgāthā is finished.
